title: The doorman who plays the odds
allegory: GELU is a doorman who lets each number in with odds that rise smoothly with its size, and the output is the average of what gets through: the number times its odds of entry.
map: a number arriving at the door
one pre-activation value x in the MLP's hidden layer
the doorman's odds, rising smoothly with size
Φ(x), the standard normal CDF: near 0 far left, near 1 far right
the average of what gets through
a strict doorman: in if positive, out if not
ReLU(x) = max(0, x), a hard switch with a corner at 0
GELU's shallow dip below zero for mildly negative x

chapters.name: Why bend at all
chapters.note: straight, then straight, is still straight

cap.1: A transformer's MLP is two straight-line maps in a row. Without a bend between them they squash into one straight map, so something has to bend.
cap.2: Linear then linear is still linear: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x. The non-linearity between the two maps is what lets the MLP compute more than one matrix could.
cap.3: A composition of affine maps is affine, so an MLP without an activation has no more expressive power than one linear layer. The activation supplies the non-linearity.

cap.1: A doorman lets each number in with odds that grow with its size: big ones nearly always, very negative ones almost never. GELU is the average result.
cap.2: GELU multiplies each input by the chance that a standard normal sample falls below it. Big positives pass almost unchanged, big negatives go to about zero, the middle is smooth.
cap.3: GELU(x) = x·Φ(x), Φ the standard normal CDF: the expectation of x·m with m ~ Bernoulli(Φ(x)), a value-dependent dropout averaged out. Smooth everywhere, unlike ReLU.

cap.1: The whole rule: the number, times the chance it gets in. That chance is a smooth S-shaped curve, near 0 on the far left and near 1 on the far right.
cap.2: Φ is the normal CDF, an S-curve like sigmoid. Libraries often compute it with a fast tanh-based approximation. Either way it is one function call.
cap.3: Φ(x) = ½(1 + erf(x/√2)); a tanh approximation is common and differs from exact GELU by well under 10⁻³. In PyTorch it is F.gelu, with an approximate='tanh' option.

cap.1: Next to ReLU, the strict doorman, they match far from zero. GELU just rounds off the corner and lets mildly negative numbers dip a little below zero.
cap.2: Far from zero they agree. Near zero GELU is smooth and slightly negative for mildly negative inputs, so its gradient there is not flatly zero.
cap.3: GELU is smooth and non-monotonic, with a shallow minimum just left of 0 and non-zero gradient for x < 0; ReLU is piecewise linear with zero gradient for x < 0.

chapters.name: Call it, move on
items: Big in, same out; very negative in, about zero out
An MLP 'neuron' is one of these outputs

cap.1: You will never need to build this by hand. Remember what it does, call the library, and spend your attention on what the MLP learns.
cap.2: It is a single call in every framework. What matters later is that each hidden unit's GELU output is what people mean by a neuron firing.
cap.3: In interpretability, 'MLP neurons' are the post-activation hidden units. Knowing GELU passes large values and near-zeroes negative ones tells you what a neuron's firing can mean.

coda.title: Make the doorman stricter and watch GELU turn into ReLU

caption.1: At −0.8 a number gets in about a fifth of the time, so the average is a little below zero. Now raise the strictness and watch the orange curve become ReLU.
caption.2: At k = 1 the orange curve is GELU. Raise k and the blue S-curve sharpens into a step, so x·Φ(kx) turns into ReLU: GELU is ReLU with the corner sanded smooth.
caption.3: x·Φ(kx) → ReLU as k → ∞. At k = 1 you get GELU's smooth, non-monotonic dip for x < 0, which is where its non-zero negative-side gradients live.

where_else: SiLU (Swish), x · sigmoid(x): the same 'value times a soft gate' idea
Gated MLPs, where one branch computes a soft gate that multiplies another
Dropout: GELU is the smooth average of a dropout whose odds depend on the value

hamming.what: A smooth ReLU: each input times the chance a standard normal sample falls below it, x·Φ(x).
hamming.when: Between the two linear maps of a transformer's MLP, as one library call.
hamming.why: The MLP needs a bend to be more than one matrix; smoothness and non-zero gradients just left of zero are the usual reasons given for this particular bend.

object.title: The sanding block
object.subtitle: A ridge whose corner is sharp at one end (ReLU) and sanded smooth at the other (GELU).

cap.1: Across the block: the number at the door. Along it: how strict the doorman is. Height: what comes out on average.
cap.2: x = input, y = strictness k, height = x·Φ(kx). Every slice across the block is one activation function.
cap.3: The family x·Φ(kx), k ∈ [0.5, 8]: a one-parameter homotopy from a very soft gate to (nearly) ReLU.

cap.1: The slice at strictness 1 is GELU: a rounded corner with a small dip on the left.
cap.2: At k = 1 the slice is exactly GELU. The dip left of zero is where small negative inputs still pass a little signal.
cap.3: The k = 1 section is GELU, with its shallow negative minimum left of 0 and a smooth derivative through the origin.

cap.1: At the far end the doorman is strict and the corner is sharp. That slice is ReLU.
cap.2: As k grows, Φ(kx) becomes a step, so the slice becomes max(0, x).
cap.3: Pointwise, x·Φ(kx) → max(0, x) as k → ∞; the negative dip shrinks towards zero.

cap.1: Far from zero every slice agrees: big numbers pass, very negative ones vanish. Only the corner changes.
cap.2: The choice of activation mostly matters near zero. Far out, all these gates behave the same.
cap.3: The members of the family differ only in a neighbourhood of 0; asymptotically all approach identity for x ≫ 0 and 0 for x ≪ 0.

cap.1: In interpretability, an MLP 'neuron' is one of these outputs. A neuron firing means its output here is large.
cap.2: Each hidden unit of the MLP produces one GELU output. Reading those outputs is how people study what individual neurons respond to.
cap.3: Post-activation MLP hidden units are the 'neurons' of mechanistic interpretability; GELU's near-zero negative side makes large positive activations the meaningful signal.

predict.q: What happens to a large positive number passing through GELU?
predict.why: For big x the odds Φ(x) are nearly 1, so GELU(x) is nearly x.

predict.q: What does GELU give for a mildly negative input like −0.5?
predict.why: It gets in some of the time, so the average is a small negative number (about −0.15).
